# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review of Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management

### Introduction
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of pregnancy-associated heart failure. Initially defined by Demakis et al. [1], PPCM is currently characterized by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [2,3] and the American Heart Association (AHA) [4] as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction—typically with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 45%—toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in women with no prior history of heart disease [3,5]. Over the last two decades, clinical registries and molecular discoveries have transformed PPCM from a poorly understood syndrome into a distinct clinical entity with targeted therapies [6,7].

### Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The incidence of PPCM exhibits significant geographic and ethnic variation, with the highest burden in Sub-Saharan Africa and among women of African descent. In the United States, Black women experience a disproportionately higher risk of PPCM and worse clinical outcomes, including lower rates of cardiac recovery [8,9]. These disparities are compounded by socioeconomic barriers, systemic inequities, and subsequent delays in diagnosis [10,11]. 

Beyond ethnicity, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy—most notably preeclampsia—are strongly associated with PPCM across global cohorts [12,13]. Registry data from the ESC EURObservational Research Programme (EORP) show that over half of women with PPCM have co-existing hypertensive disorders [14]. Other established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, and twin pregnancies [15].

### Pathophysiology
The contemporary understanding of PPCM involves a vascular-hormonal process triggered by late-pregnancy physiology in genetically predisposed individuals. Late in pregnancy and early postpartum, increased oxidative stress triggers the lysosomal protease cathepsin D, which cleaves full-length prolactin from the pituitary gland into a toxic 16-kDa fragment [16,17]. This fragment is anti-angiogenic, pro-apoptotic, and pro-inflammatory, inducing microvascular endothelial damage and cardiomyocyte apoptosis [16]. 

Simultaneously, late-pregnancy placental secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), which antagonizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), Netrin, and other angiogenic factors, exacerbates this cardiotoxic angiogenic imbalance [18]. These cascades are further mediated by downstream microRNAs, specifically miR-146a, which impairs cardiomyocyte metabolism [19]. Furthermore, genetic sequencing has revealed that approximately 10% to 15% of women with PPCM carry truncating variants in sarcomeric genes, most commonly the titin gene (*TTN*), highlighting a shared genetic architecture with dilated cardiomyopathy [20,21].

### Diagnosis and Clinical Presentation
The clinical presentation of PPCM ranges from mild heart failure symptoms (e.g., exertional dyspnea, cough, orthopnea, pedal edema) to cardiogenic shock or sudden cardiac arrest. Because these symptoms mimic normal physiological changes of late pregnancy, diagnosis is frequently delayed [10]. Initial evaluation should include an electrocardiogram, which commonly displays non-specific ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities [22], and measurement of natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP). Transthoracic echocardiography remains the gold standard, showing an LVEF < 45% [2,3].

### Management and Therapeutic Strategies
Therapy depends on the timing of presentation and hemodynamic stability. For antepartum presentation, guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure must be carefully tailored; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are strictly contraindicated due to fetotoxicity [2,3]. Standard beta-blockers and diuretics can be used cautiously before delivery [3]. 

The prospective IPAC study demonstrated that LVEF and LV end-diastolic diameter at presentation are key predictors of recovery [23], while the ESC EORP registry provides robust real-world data on clinical presentations and outcomes [24]. 

A major breakthrough in PPCM therapy is the use of bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 receptor agonist that blocks pituitary prolactin secretion. A landmark multicenter randomized trial confirmed that adding bromocriptine to standard heart failure therapy improves LVEF recovery [25]. Due to the pro-thrombotic state of the peripartum period, bromocriptine must always be paired with prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation [3,25]. In cases of cardiogenic shock, inotropes like levosimendan [26] and temporary mechanical circulatory support or a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) may be utilized to bridge patients to recovery or device implantation [27].

### Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies
While many women experience significant cardiac recovery within six months, long-term prognosis varies. Breastfeeding is safe in stable patients who have recovered cardiac function and does not impair myocardial recovery [28]. However, subsequent pregnancies pose a major clinical challenge. For women with persistent LV dysfunction, subsequent pregnancy is associated with high rates of heart failure relapse and maternal mortality, and is strongly contraindicated [29,30]. Even in those with recovered LV function (LVEF ≥ 50%), there is a 20% to 30% risk of recurrence, requiring rigorous preconception counseling, multidisciplinary care, and close monitoring during future gestations [29,30].
